name: HTTP header order and casing
plain: The set and order of request headers is different for each browser and HTTP library.
meaning: Chrome, Firefox and Safari send Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding and Sec-* headers in distinct orders; scripted clients (requests, Go, Node fetch) differ. Mismatches versus the User-Agent flag bots.

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from the order of request headers
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens with every page request
can: Compare the order and casing of header lines with known browsers
Spot scripts and bots that use plain code libraries
Flag a browser name that does not match the headers
cannot: Know your name or account from it
See your files or other tabs
Tell two people on the same browser version apart

story.what_it_is: The order of the info your browser sends to a site reveals which browser it is.
story.for_you: You never see it. Each browser sends the same pieces in a slightly different order, like a signature. A site can tell Chrome from Firefox from a script even if the browser claims otherwise.
story.for_makers: Bot defense vendors use header order as a quick way to catch scripts pretending to be browsers. It is also a fingerprint input, since software versions and add-ons leave marks.

use_cases.example: A bot defense checks if the header order matches the browser claim, and blocks scripts that fake Chrome.
A game login page blocks credential stuffing tools that send headers in an odd order.
A sneaker or ticket site spots scalper bots by header order before the sale begins.
An ad platform filters click fraud from scripts with the wrong header signature.
A traffic report separates real browsers from crawlers.
A streaming site stops account sharing and scraping tools by headers.

technical_bounds: Proxies and CDNs can reorder headers
